title: WPSB/392/2017 of Sudhir Kumar Vs State Of Uttarakhand AND OTHERS

paras.text:
Reserved Judgment
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
REVIEW APPLICATION No. 50 of 2019
IN
Writ Petition (S/B) No. 392 of 2017
Sudhir Kumar ...Petitioner
vs.
State of Uttarakhand & others ...Respondents
Mr. Vinay Kumar, learned counsel for the petitioner.
Mr. B.S. Parihar, learned Standing Counsel for the State of Uttarakhand.
Mr. B.D. Kandpal, learned counsel for the Uttarakhand Public Service Commission.
Mr. K.P. Upadhyaya, learned Senior Counsel assisted by Mr. B.S. Adhikari, learned counsel for
the review applicant.
 Reserved on : 23.08.2019
Delivered on: 02.09.2019

45. AIR 1980 SC 674
Coram: Hon'ble Ramesh Ranganathan, C.J.
 Hon'ble Lok Pal Singh, J.
Ramesh Ranganathan, C.J.
 Are posts in the general category not available to be filled up by
members of the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the other

2
backward classes on their merit? As a corollary thereto, are posts
horizontally reserved in favour of ex-servicemen in the general
category not available to ex-servicemen belonging to the scheduled
castes, the scheduled tribes, and the other backward classes on their
own merit?
2. Despite the challenge to the order under review (i.e. order in
Writ Petition (S/B) No.392 of 2017 dated 11.12.2018), being repelled
by the Supreme Court, in its order in Special Leave Petition (C) No.
7801 of 2019 dated 15.04.2019, and the review application filed
thereafter (i.e. Review Application No.567 of 2019) by the Public
Service Commission having been dismissed by order dated
19.07.2019, the review applicant herein still contends that he is
entitled to invoke the review jurisdiction of this Court, since it is the
Uttarakhand Public Service Commission which had preferred an
appeal, against the order under review, before the Supreme Court, and
had filed the review application before this Court thereafter, and not
the review applicant (who was the fourth respondent in the writ
petition).
3. In M. Satyanarayana Murthy v. Mandal Revenue, Officer-cum-Land Acquisition Officer1
, the Supreme Court held that
recourse to successive review petitions against the same order is not
permissible, more so where there is no error apparent on the record ;
the petitioners were unnecessarily taking liberties; and the filing of a
second review petition was an abuse of the process of the court.
Thereafter, in Chandro Devi v. Union of India2
, the Supreme Court
held that the appellants had earlier filed a review petition which was
dismissed and, thereafter, they had filed a second review petition,
which was rightly dismissed by the High Court as not maintainable
being a second review petition.
4. We have our reservations whether a fresh and second review
application can be entertained against the very same order, even if it
be by another respondent in the Writ Petition, more so as the SLP

3
preferred thereagainst was not entertained by the Supreme Court, and
the review petition filed before us thereafter, by the Public Service
Commissioner, was dismissed. In view of the importance of the
questions raised, and to put the controversy that members of the
Scheduled Castes are ineligible to compete on their merit for posts
horizontally reserved under the general category, to rest, we shall
proceed and examine the contentions urged on the behalf of the 4th
respondent-review applicant on its merits, instead of non-suiting him
on the ground that a second review application, against the very same
order, may not lie.
5. The grounds on which this review application is filed is that,
while vertical reservation in favour of the scheduled castes, the
scheduled tribes and the other backward classes, may require posts in
the general category to be made available to members of these
reserved categories on their merit, such a benefit is not available to the
vertically reserved categories, (the scheduled castes, the scheduled
tribes and the other backward classes), in posts horizontally reserved
in favour of women, the physically handicapped, the ex-servicemen
etc in the general category.
6. Before examining the contentions urged, and the judgments
relied upon, on behalf of the 4th respondent, it is necessary to briefly
note the facts leading upto the filing of the present review application.
Writ Petition (S/B) No. 392 of 2017 was filed seeking to quash the
selection of the review applicant herein (the 4th respondent in the writ
petition) to the post of Deputy Collector, under horizontal reservation
provided in favour of the ex-servicemen in the general category,
pursuant to the select-list dated 27.07.2017. Reservation, in favour of
ex-servicemen, was provided in the subject selection process only
under the general category, and not under the scheduled caste
category.
7. Both the writ petitioner and the 4th respondent-review applicant
belonged to the ex-service men category. While the writ petitioner

4
was a member of the scheduled castes, the 4th respondent-review
applicant did not fall within any of the reserved categories (i.e. the
scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the other backward
classes). While the writ petitioner secured 807 marks, the 4th
respondent-review applicant secured 776 marks i.e. 31 marks lesser
than the writ petitioner. However on the ground that the writ
petitioner, though more meritorious than the 4th respondent-review
applicant, belonged to the scheduled castes, and horizontal reservation
for ex-servicemen had not been provided in the scheduled caste
category but only in the general category, the Uttarakhand Public
Service Commission selected the review-applicant for appointment to
the post of Deputy Collector, instead of the writ petitioner.
8. On such selection being subjected to challenge in Writ
proceedings, we had, in our order in Writ Petition (S/B) No.392 of
2017 dated 11.12.2018, held that vertical reservation, not exceeding
50%, can be provided in favour of the backward sections of society
such as the other backward classes, the scheduled castes and the
scheduled tribes; horizontal reservation is permissible in each of the
aforesaid categories, as also in the general category, in favour of
women, physically handicapped, ex-servicemen etc; horizontal
reservation can be provided in the general category also; all applicants
are entitled to compete for the horizontally reserved posts, on their
merit, provided they fall under the categories for which horizontal
reservation is provided; consequently all candidates, who belong to
the ex-servicemen category, are entitled to be considered on their
merit, to posts earmarked in favour of ex-servicemen under the
general category, irrespective of whether they belong to the other
backward classes, the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes or do not
belong to any of these reserved categories; and the most meritorious,
among the ex-servicemen, is required to be selected and appointed to
the post earmarked for ex-servicemen under the general category.
9. We had, following the law laid down by the Supreme Court in
Rajesh Kumar Daria vs. Rajasthan Public Service3
, observed that

5
members of the reserved category (i.e. the other backward classes, the
scheduled castes and the scheduled tribes), were entitled to compete,
on their own merit, for selection and appointment to posts in the
general category; applying the law laid down by the Supreme Court,
in Rajesh Kumar Daria3
, to the facts of the present case, would
require the Public Service Commission to fill up general category
posts in the first instance, solely on the basis of the inter-se merit of
candidates; such general category posts would also include posts
horizontally reserved under the said category i.e. posts earmarked for
ex-servicemen, under the general category, must also be filled up with
the most meritorious ex-serviceman, irrespective of whether or not he
belongs to a reserved category (the other backward classes, the
scheduled castes or the scheduled tribes); and the mere fact that the
posts were horizontally reserved in favour of ex-servicemen under the
general category, and were not reserved in favour of the other
backward classes, the scheduled castes or the scheduled tribes, could
not have resulted in a more meritorious scheduled caste candidate,
who was also an ex-serviceman, being deprived of selection, under the
ex-servicemen quota in the general category, strictly on the basis of
his merit.
10. After noting that a similar contention was also raised before the
Allahabad High Court in Brijendra Deo Mishra vs. Public Service
Commission, U.P. Allahabad4
, we had concluded holding that the
Uttarakhand Public Service Commission had erred in not appointing
the writ petitioner in the post earmarked for ex-servicemen under the
general category, though he had secured more marks than the fourth
respondent (review applicant herein), solely on the ground that he
belonged to the scheduled castes. The selection of the fourth
respondent was set-aside, and the Public Service Commission was
directed to forthwith forward the writ petitioner's name to the
Government for necessary orders to be issued appointing him in the
post of Deputy Collector under the quota of ex-servicemen earmarked
under the general category.

6
11. Aggrieved by the said order, the Uttarakhand Public Service
Commission carried the matter in appeal to the Supreme Court filing
SLP (C) No. 7801 of 2019. In its order in SLP (C) No. 7801 of 2019
dated 15.04.2019, the Supreme Court observed that, after arguing the
matter at some length, the learned Senior Counsel, appearing on
behalf of the Commission, had sought permission to withdraw the
Special Leave Petition and move the High Court to seek clarification
whether, while complying with the impugned order, the 4th respondent
(review applicant) could also be accommodated, along with the first
respondent-writ petitioner, by the Public Service Commission. Having
regard to the submission made at the Bar, the Special Leave Petition
was disposed of as withdrawn with liberty as sought for. The
Supreme Court also noted the submission, urged on behalf of the first
respondent-writ petitioner, that he would seek adjournment of three
weeks in the pending contempt petition.
12. Thereafter, the Uttarakhand Public Service Commission filed
Review Application No. 567 of 2019 in Writ Petition (S/B) No. 392 of
2017. We had, in our order in Review Application No. 567 of 2019
dated 19.07.2019, expressed our disinclination to issue any direction,
as sought for by the Uttarakhand Public Service Commission, to
adjust the 4th respondent-review applicant also in the post of Deputy
Collector along with the writ petitioner, and had opined that the order
passed by us did not disable the Commission from taking such action
as they considered appropriate, and in accordance with law.
13. Sri K.P. Upadhyay, learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf
of the 4th respondent-review applicant, would submit that unlike
vertical reservation, which is provided in favour of the scheduled
castes, the scheduled tribes and the other backward classes under
Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India, horizontal reservation, in
favour of ex-servicemen, is provided under Article 16(1) of the
Constitution of India; the tests, which would apply in providing
reservation under Article 16(4), would not apply to horizontal

7
reservation under Article 16(1); while the principles governing
vertical reservation is that reservation is in addition to merit, the said
test would have no application to horizontal reservation; horizontal
reservation is required to be provided separately for each category (i.e.
the general category, the other backward classes, the scheduled castes
and the scheduled tribes); such horizontal reservation, prescribed for a
particular category, cannot be shifted to another category; in the
present case, horizontal reservation in favour of ex-servicemen is
provided under the general category, and not for posts earmarked for
the scheduled castes; since horizontal reservation has not been
provided under the scheduled caste category, the writ petitioner, who
is a member of the scheduled castes, is disentitled from claiming the
benefit of horizontal reservation provided in favour of ex-servicemen
under the general category; the advertisement stipulated that the
person, who claims the benefit of reservation, cannot change his
option later; since the writ petitioner had sought the benefit of
reservation as a member of the scheduled castes, he cannot now claim
the benefit of horizontal reservation in favour of ex-servicemen under
the general category; the conditions stipulated in the advertisement are
binding on the writ petitioner also; while the Division Bench had in its
order, no doubt, taken note of the provisions of the Uttar Pradesh
Public Services (Reservation for Physically Handicapped, Dependents
of Freedom Fighters and Ex-Servicemen) Act, 1993, an erroneous
construction was placed on the relevant provisions of the said Act;
and since the order under review suffers from an error apparent on the
face of record, and is contrary to the law laid down by the Supreme
Court in Rajesh Kumar Daria3
; Public Service Commission,
Uttaranchal vs. Mamta Bisht and Ors5
; State of U.P. Vs. Rajeev
Kumar6
; Anil Kumar Gupta and Ors. vs. State of U.P. and Ors7
;
Rajeev Kumar Vs. State of U.P.8
; Ashish Kumar Pandey vs. State
of U.P. and others9
; and the order of the Full Bench of the Allahabad
High Court, in Ajay Kumar vs. State of U.P. and others10, the order
under review must be set aside and the review application must be
allowed.

8
14. The premise, on which the submissions urged on behalf of the
review applicant is based, is that horizontal reservation provided in
favour of ex-servicemen, under the general category, is not available
to ex-servicemen belonging to the scheduled castes, the scheduled
tribes, and the other backward classes, even if they are ex-servicemen
who are more meritorious than the ex-servicemen who do not belong
to these reserved categories. This, in turn, is based on the premise that
posts horizontally reserved in favour of ex-servicemen, under the
general category, are available only to the un-reserved category i.e.
candidates other than those belonging to the scheduled castes, the
scheduled tribes, and the other backward classes. Both these premises
are flawed.
15. Reservation, under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India, is
provided in favour of the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and
the other backward classes, as they are socially and educationally
backward. There is no reservation in the general category and posts in
the general category are open to all, including the scheduled castes,
the scheduled tribes and the other backward classes, to be filled up on
the basis of the inter-se merit of all the candidates. Reservation under
Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India, as has been held by the
Supreme Court in Indira Sawhney Vs. Union of India11, is in
addition to merit i.e. while a member of the scheduled castes, the
scheduled tribes and the other backward classes are entitled to
compete, on their own merit, under the general category, they would,
in addition, be entitled for reservation under Article 16(4) of the
Constitution of India in posts earmarked for the specific reserved
categories i.e. separately for the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes
and the other backward classes. For example, if a member of the
scheduled castes stands first in the order of merit, he would be
required to be selected and appointed in a post in the general category,
and not in posts reserved for members of the scheduled castes, since
he is entitled to be appointed to posts under the general category on
his own merit, and not as a member of the scheduled castes.

9
16. The situation does not change much in the case of horizontal
reservation either. Such horizontal reservation, under Article 16(1) of
the Constitution, is provided in favour of Uttarakhand women, the
physically handicapped, the ex-servicemen, dependents of freedom
fighters from Uttarakhand etc. Horizontal reservation can, no doubt,
be provided under separate categories i.e. the general category, the
scheduled caste category, the scheduled tribe category and the other
backward classes category. Horizontal reservation provided, for
instance to women, under all these categories would result in posts
reserved for women under the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes
and the other backward classes categories, not being, ordinarily,
available to women who do not belong to each of these categories.
17. The converse, however, is not true. Horizontal reservation, in
favour of women in the general category, is available to all women
irrespective of their caste or social status. The posts, horizontally
reserved in favour of women in the general category, are made
available to all women candidates strictly in the order of their merit.
The only distinction between vertical reservation and horizontal
reservation is that, if the posts horizontally reserved in favour of
women in each of these categories is filled up by women equal to or
exceeding the quota horizontally reserved in their favour, then women
lower in rank would not be entitled to claim the benefit of horizontal
reservation contending that women, who have secured appointment on
their own merit, should be excluded from consideration for posts
horizontally reserved in favour of women. While the principle of
vertical reservation, in favour of the backward classes under Article
16(4) being in addition to merit, may not strictly apply to horizontal
reservation provided under Article 16(1), that does not mean that
posts, horizontally reserved under the general category, are
unavailable to the backward Sections (i.e the SCs, STs and OBCs) in
whose favour reservation is provided under Article 16(4) of the
Constitution. Posts under the general category are available to all,
including those who belong to the scheduled castes, the scheduled

10
tribes and the other backward classes. Consequently posts,
horizontally reserved in favour of ex-servicemen in the general
category, would be available to all ex-servicemen irrespective of
whether they belong to the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes, the
other backward classes or other categories, and should be filled up
strictly in the order of their inter-se merit.
18. A similar test, as is applicable while providing horizontal
reservation in favour of women, would also apply in providing
horizontal reservation in favour of ex-servicemen. For instance if out
of the ten posts in the general category, one post is horizontally
reserved in favour of ex-servicemen, all candidates, irrespective of
their caste status, must be arranged strictly in the order of their inter se
merit; and, if there are one or more ex-servicemen in the top ten most
meritorious candidates, then nothing more is required to be done.
However, in case there are no ex-servicemen among the top ten
candidates, the Public Service Commission is then obliged to pick-up
the most meritorious ex-serviceman, even if he does not fall within the
top ten, and replace the tenth candidate in the merit list by him. In the
present case, the last candidate in the merit list, under the general or
open category, had secured 818 marks, and both the writ petitioner,
and the fourth respondent-review applicant, had secured lesser marks
than him, and were lower than him in merit. Since none of the
candidates who secured 818 marks or more belonged to the ex-servicemen category, the Public Service Commission was required to
substitute the candidate who secured 818 marks in the general
category, with the most meritorious ex-serviceman, even though he
had secured lesser marks.
19. The writ petitioner, an ex-serviceman who had secured 807
marks, stood higher in the order of merit than the fourth respondent-review applicant who had secured only 776 marks. Consequently the
writ petitioner, being the most meritorious ex-servicemen, ought to
have been selected and appointed to the post reserved in favour of ex-

11
servicemen under the general category, and not the fourth respondent-review applicant who had secured 31 marks lesser than him.
20. The Public Service Commission, however, selected the fourth
respondent-review applicant on the erroneous premise that the post,
horizontally reserved in favour of ex-servicemen under the general
category, was not available to ex-servicemen belonging to the
scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the other backward classes,
even if they were found to be more meritorious than the other
candidates who did not belong to any of these categories. That, in
effect, is an indirect mode of introduction of communal reservation
which the Supreme Court had frowned upon in State of Madras v.
Champakam Dorairajan12. While we are satisfied that the order
under review does not suffer from any error, much less an error
apparent, warranting its review, we must however take note of the law
declared, by the Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court, in the
judgments relied upon on behalf of the fourth respondent-review
applicant.
21. In Anil Kumar Gupta7
, in the initial notification fifteen per
cent Special (horizontal) reservation was treated as vertical
reservation, along with reservation in favour of the other backward
classes, the scheduled castes and the scheduled tribes; with the
decision of the Supreme Court in Swati Gupta vs. State of U.P. &
others13, these special reservations became horizontal reservation;
candidates, who had applied under any of the said Special (horizontal)
reservations, were asked to specify whether they belonged to the
scheduled tribes, the scheduled castes, the other backward classes or
to the open competition category; out of 2130 candidates, who had
applied against the five special reservation categories, only nine
belonged to the other backward classes; none belonged to the
scheduled tribes or the scheduled castes which meant that, but for nine
candidates, all the rest under the special categories were from the
general/non-reserved category; 110 out of 112 special reservation
candidates had been accommodated only in the General category, and

12
none in the OBC, SC OR ST category; the authorities in charge had
first taken up special category reservations and filled them up; of the
112 candidates, 101 were from what may be called the "unreserved
category" while nine candidates belonged to the other backward
classes; as the nine candidates, belonging to the other backward
classes, had secured equal marks with the general candidates, and
were selected on merit in the general category, they were treated as
general category candidates; the result was that out of 112 seats
reserved for special categories, 110 seats were taken away from the
open competition (OC) category, thus leaving only 263 seats for the
general candidates, i.e., OC candidates not belonging to any of the
special reservations; and it was this method of filling up seats which
had been challenged in the writ petitions.
22. The contentions, urged on behalf of the petitioners in Anil
Kumar Gupta7
, were twofold: (i) special reservation seats should be
distributed and allocated proportionately among the social, i.e.,
vertical reservation categories; had it been so done, only fifty-six
candidates belonging to special reservation categories could be
accommodated in the OC category; but the respondents had
accommodated 110 special reservation candidates in the OC category,
an excess of fifty-four seats; and these fifty-four seats must be taken
away from the special reservation categories and allotted to OC
candidates, not belonging to any special reservation category; and (ii)
the procedure prescribed for filling up vacancies was equally illegal
which had also resulted in the diminution of seats available for the OC
category. With respect to the first contention, the respondents had
contended that fifteen percent reservation, in favour of special
categories (special reservation) was an overall reservation, and not a
compartmentalised reservation; these special reservations were not
divided proportionately among the vertical (social) reservation
categories; and these special reservation candidates had to be provided
fifteen per cent of the total seats (i.e. 112 seats) overall, whether by

13
adjusting them against any of the social/vertical reservations or
otherwise. It is in this context that the Supreme Court observed :
 "......On a careful consideration of the revised
notification of December 17, 1994 and the aforementioned
corrigendum issued by the Lucknow University, we are of the
opinion that in view of the ambiguous language employed
therein, it is not possible to give a definite answer to the
question whether the horizontal reservations are overall
reservations or compartmentalised reservations. We may
explain these two expressions. Where the seats reserved for
horizontal reservations are proportionately divided among
the vertical (social) reservations and are not
interransferable, it would be a case of compartmentalised
reservations. We may illustrate what we say: Take this very
case; out of the total 746 seats, 112 seats (representing
fifteen percent) should be filled by special reservation
candidates; at the same time, the social reservation in
favour of Other Backward Classes is 27% which means 201
seats for O.B.Cs.; if the 112 special reservation seats are
also divided proportionately as between O.C., O.B.C., S.C.
and S.T., 30 seats would be allocated to the O.B.C. category;
in other words, thirty special category students can be
accommodated in the O.B.C. category; but say only ten
special reservation candidates belonging to O.B.C. are
available, then these ten candidates will, of course, be
allocated among O.B.C. quota but the remaining twenty
seats cannot be transferred to O.C. category (they will be
available for O.B.C. candidates only) or for that matter, to
any other category; this would be so whether requisite
number of special reservation candidates (56 out of 373) are
available in O.C. category or not; the special reservation
would be a water tight compartment in each of the vertical
reservation classes (O.C., O.B.C., S.C. and S.T.). As against
this, what happens in the overall reservation is that while
allocating the special reservation students to their respective
social reservation category, the overall reservation in favour
of special reservation categories has yet to be honoured.
This means that in the above illustration, the twenty
remaining seats would be transferred to O.C. category
which means that the number of special reservation
candidates in O.C. category would be 56+20=76. Further, if
no special reservation candidate belonging to S.C. and S.T.
is available then the proportionate number of seats meant
for special reservation candidates in S.C. and S.T. also get
transferred to O.C. category. The result would be that 102
special reservation candidates have to be accommodated in
the O.C. category to complete their quota of 112. The
converse may also happen, which will prejudice the
candidates in the reserved categories. It is, of course,

14
obvious that the inter-se quota between O.C., O.B.C., S.C.
and S.T. will not be altered.............
".............Now, coming to the correctness of the
procedure prescribed by the revised notification for filling up
the seats, it was wrong to direct the fifteen percent special
reservation seats to be filled up first and then take up the
O.C.(merit) quota (followed by filling of O.B.C., S.C. and
S.T. quotas). The proper and correct course is to first fill up
the O.C. quota (50%) on the basis of merit; then fill up each
of the social reservation quotas, i.e., S.C., S.T. and B.C; the
third step would be to find out how many candidates
belonging to special reservations have been selected on the
above basis. If the quota fixed for horizontal reservations is
already satisfied - in case it is an overall horizontal
reservation - no further question arises. But if it is not so
satisfied, the requisite number of special reservation
candidates shall have to be taken and
adjusted/accommodated against their respective social
reservation categories by deleting the corresponding
number of candidates therefrom, (If, however, it is a case of
compartmentalised horizontal reservation, then the process
of verification and adjustment/accommodation as stated
above should be applied separately to each of the vertical
reservations. In such a case, the reservation of fifteen
percent in favour of special categories, overall, may be
satisfied or may not be satisfied). Because the revised
notification provided for a different method of filling the seats,
it has contributed partly to the unfortunate situation where the
entire special reservation quota has been allocated and adjusted
almost exclusively against the O.C. quota.
In this connection, we must reiterate what this Court has
said in Indira Sawhney11. While holding that what may be
called "horizontal reservation" can be provided under Clause
(1) of Article 16, the majority judgment administered the
following caution in para 744:
"(B)ut at the same time, one thing is clear. It is in very
exceptional situation - and not for all and sundry reasons -
that any further reservations of whatever kind, should be
provided under Clause (1). In such cases, the State has to
satisfy, if called upon, that making such a provision was
necessary (in public interest) to redress the specific
situation. The very presence of Clause (4) should act as a
damper upon the propensity to create further classes
deserving special treatment. The reason for saying so is very
simple. If reservations are made both under Clause (4) as
well as under (1), the vacancies available for free
competition as well as reserved categories would be
correspondingly whittled down and that is not a reasonable
thing to do".

15
Though the said observations were made with reference
to Clauses (1) and (4) of Article 16, the same apply with equal
force to Clauses (1) and (4) of Article 15 as well. In this case,
the reservation of fifteen percent of seats for special categories
was on very high side. As pointed out above, two categories out
of them representing six percent out of fifteen percent are really
reservations under Article 15(4), wrongly treated as
reservations under Article 15(1). Even otherwise, the special
reservation would be nine percent. The respondents would be
well advised to keep in mind the admonition administered by
this Court and ensure that the special reservations (horizontal
reservations) are kept at the minimum...."
(emphasis supplied)
23. The law declared by the Supreme Court, in Anil Kumar Gupta
and Ors7
, is that, where seats reserved horizontally are
proportionately divided among the vertical (social) reservations, and
are not inter-transferable, it would be a case of compartmentalised
reservations; the special reservation would be a water tight
compartment in each of the vertical reservation classes (O.C., O.B.C.,
S.C. and S.T.); as against this, what would happen in the overall
reservation was that, while allocating the special reservation seats to
their respective social reservation category, the overall reservation in
favour of special reservation categories had to be honoured; the inter-se quota between the O.C, the O.B.C, the S.C. and the S.T. should not
be altered; it was wrong to direct the fifteen percent special
reservation seats to be filled up first, and then take up the O.C.(merit)
quota (followed by filling of O.B.C., S.C. and S.T. quotas); the proper
and correct course was to first fill up the O.C. quota (50%) on the
basis of merit; then fill up each of the social reservation quotas, i.e.,
S.C., S.T. and B.C; the third step would be to find out how many
candidates belonging to special reservations have been selected on the
above basis; if the quota fixed for horizontal reservations is already
satisfied, in case it is an overall horizontal reservation, no further
question arose; but, if it was not so satisfied, the requisite number of
special reservation candidates should be taken and adjusted/
accommodated against their respective social reservation categories
by deleting the corresponding number of candidates therefrom; if it

16
was a case of compartmentalised horizontal reservation, then the
process of verification and adjustment/ accommodation should be
applied separately to each of the vertical reservations; and, in such a
case, the reservation of fifteen percent in favour of special categories,
overall, may or not be satisfied.
24. In Rajesh Kumar Daria3
, the appellants before the Supreme
Court had contended that women candidates were selected in excess
of their reservation quota; though the rules provided for horizontal
reservation of 20% for women category-wise, the public service
commission had wrongly applied the principles of vertical reservation,
and had selected women in excess of the quota, thereby denying
selection of the appellants, and other male candidates, though they had
secured higher marks than the selected women candidates, and would
have been selected but for the excess reservation provided in favour of
women candidates.
25. After taking note of its earlier judgments in Indira Sawhney11
,
and Anil Kumar Gupta7
, the Supreme Court held that, unlike vertical
reservation where members of the scheduled castes would be entitled
for reservation in posts reserved for the scheduled castes, excluding a
member of the scheduled castes who had secured appointment on their
own merit, such a principle would not apply in the case of horizontal
reservation; and, in case the quota reserved for women category is
fulfilled on the basis of sufficient women having secured appointment
on their own merit, women lower in merit would not be entitled for
the benefit of horizontal reservation. The Supreme Court, thereafter,
observed:-
"........The second relates to the difference between the
nature of vertical reservation and horizontal reservation.
Social reservations in favour of SC, ST and OBC under Article
16(4) are "vertical reservations". Special reservations in favour
of physically handicapped, women, etc., under Articles 16(1) or
15(3) are "horizontal reservations". Where a vertical
reservation is made in favour of a Backward Class under
Article 16(4), the candidates belonging to such Backward

17
Class, may compete for non-reserved posts and if they are
appointed to the non-reserved posts on their own merit, their
number will not be counted against the quota reserved for
respective Backward Class. Therefore, if the number of SC
candidates, who by their own merit, get selected to open
competition vacancies, equals or even exceeds the percentage
of posts reserved for SC candidates, it cannot be said that the
reservation quota for SCs has been filled. The entire
reservation quota will be intact and available in addition to
those selected under open competition category. (Vide Indra
Sawhney: (1992) Supp. (3) SCC 217, R.K. Sabharwal v. State
of Punjab: (1995) 2 SCC 745, Union of India v. Virpal Singh
Chauhan: 1995 (6) SCC 684 and Ritesh R. Sah v. Dr. Y.L.
Yamul: (1996) 3 SCC 253). But the aforesaid principle
applicable to vertical (social) reservations will not apply to
horizontal (special) reservations. Where a special reservation
for women is provided within the social reservation for
Scheduled Castes, the proper procedure is first to fill up the
quota for Scheduled Castes in order of merit and then find out
the number of candidates among them who belong to the
special reservation group of "Scheduled Caste women". If the
number of women in such list is equal to or more than the
number of special reservation quota, then there is no need for
further selection towards the special reservation quota. Only if
there is any shortfall, the requisite number of Scheduled Caste
women shall have to be taken by deleting the corresponding
number of candidates from the bottom of the list relating to
Scheduled Castes. To this extent, horizontal (special)
reservation differs from vertical (social) reservation. Thus
women selected on merit within the vertical reservation quota
will be counted against the horizontal reservation for women.
Let us illustrate by an example:
If 19 posts are reserved for SCs (of which the quota
for women is four), 19 SC candidates shall have to be first
listed in accordance with merit, from out of the successful
eligible candidates. If such list of 19 candidates contains
four SC woman candidates, then there is no need to disturb
the list by including any further SC woman candidate. On
the other hand, if the list of 19 SC candidates contains only
two woman candidates, then the next two SC woman
candidates in accordance with merit, will have to be
included in the list and corresponding number of candidates
from the bottom of such list shall have to be deleted, so as to
ensure that the final 19 selected SC candidates contain four
woman SC candidates. (But if the list of 19 SC candidates
contains more than four woman candidates, selected on own
merit, all of them will continue in the list and there is no
question of deleting the excess woman candidates on the
ground that "SC women" have been selected in excess of the
prescribed internal quota of four.)

18
In this case, the number of candidates to be selected under
general category (open competition), were 59, out of which 11
were earmarked for women. When the first 59 from among the
261 successful candidates were taken and listed as per merit, it
contained 11 woman candidates, which was equal to the quota for
"general category women". There was thus no need for any
further selection of woman candidates under the special
reservation for women. But what RPSC did was to take only the
first 48 candidates in the order of merit (which contained 11
women) and thereafter, fill the next 11 posts under the general
category with woman candidates. As a result, we find that among
59 general category candidates in all 22 women have been selected
consisting of eleven woman candidates selected on their own merit
(candidates at Sl. Nos. 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 19, 21, 25, 31, 35 and 41 of the
selection list) and another eleven (candidates at Sl. Nos. 54, 61, 62,
63, 66, 74, 75, 77, 78, 79 and 80 of the selection list) included under
reservation quota for "general category women". This is clearly
impermissible. The process of selections made by RPSC amounts
to treating the 20% reservation for women as a vertical
reservation, instead of being a horizontal reservation within the
vertical reservation.
Similarly, we find that in regard to 24 posts for OBC, 19
candidates were selected by RPSC in accordance with merit from
among OBC candidates which included three woman candidates.
Thereafter, another five women were selected under the category
of "OBC women", instead of adding only two which was the
shortfall. Thus there were in all 8 women candidates among the 24
OBC candidates found in the selection list. The proper course was
to list 24 OBC candidates as per the merit and then find out
number of woman candidates among them, and only fill the
shortfall to make up the quota of five for women......"
(emphasis supplied)
26. The law laid down by the Supreme Court, in Rajesh Kumar
Daria3
, is that where special (horizontal) reservation for women is
provided, within the social reservation for the Scheduled Castes, the
proper procedure is first to fill up the quota for the Scheduled Castes
in the order of merit, and then find out the number of candidates
among them who belong to the special (horizontal) reservation group
of "Scheduled Caste women"; if the number of women, in such a list
is equal to or more than the number of special (horizontal) reservation
quota, then there is no need for further selection towards the special
(horizontal) reservation quota; only if there is any shortfall, the

19
requisite number of Scheduled Caste women should be taken by
deleting the corresponding number of candidates from the bottom of
the list relating to the Scheduled Castes; to this extent, horizontal
(special) reservation differs from vertical (social) reservation; and
women selected on merit, within the vertical reservation quota, will be
counted against the horizontal reservation for women.
27. In Mamta Bisht5
, the Commission had issued an advertisement
inviting application for 35 posts of Civil Judge, (Junior Division)
providing both horizontal and vertical reservation. However 42 posts
were filled up. Out of the 42 posts which were filled up, 26 were filled
up from the general category, and 16 from the reserved category. The
respondents before the Supreme Court had contended that women
candidates, higher in the order of merit, should have been selected in
the general category, in which event posts reserved in favour of
women would have been available to her though she was lower in the
order of merit than those other women who were selected and
appointed against posts earmarked in favour of Uttarakhand women.
The Uttarakhand High Court had held that, as the last selected
candidate receiving the benefit of horizontal reservation had secured
marks more than the last selected general category candidate, she
ought to have been appointed against the vacancy in the general
category. The Supreme Court held that the High Court had allowed
the Writ Petition only on the ground that horizontal reservation is also
to be applied as vertical reservation in favour of the reserved category;
and the view taken by the High Court, on the application of horizontal
reservation, was contrary to the law laid down in Rajesh Kumar
Daria3
.
28. The law laid down in Mamta Bisht5
 is that horizontal
reservation cannot be applied as vertical reservation in favour of the
reserved categories; and women candidates higher in the order of
merit, (in whose favour horizontal reservation is provided and who
were selected in the general category), cannot be excluded in

20
computing the number of posts to be horizontally reserved in favour
of women in the general category.
29. In Rajeev Kumar8 a Division Bench of the Allahabad High
Court, following the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Rajesh
Kumar Daria3 and Anil Kumar Gupta7
, observed that, for
horizontal reservation, the candidates, who have been selected
according to vertical reservation, shall be placed in their respective

would be given category-wise; the quota of female category
candidates of 20 percent in a particular category cannot be enhanced
by clubbing together the total number of posts; only if there is any
shortfall, the requisite number of reserved category females
candidates shall have to be taken by deleting the corresponding
number of candidates from the bottom of the list relating to such
category; the Rules do not allow the respondent-State Government to
extend the benefit of reservation beyond 20 percent in the respective

device to recruit candidates of the female category, even if they are
less meritorious, in order to complete such horizontal reservation for
which candidates are not available in other categories; and there could
not be a pooling of women category candidates in excess of 20
percent against the strength of a category, as horizontal reservation in
the instant case is compartmentalized; if the female category
candidates are more meritorious than the male category candidates,
then they will be entitled to be accommodated in their respective
categories according to their merit, but again their merit will have to
be higher than the male category candidates; women can compete
with men for the balance of 80 percent seats within their category on
merit, but not with the aid of the logic of saturating the unfilled seats,
of 20 percent horizontal reservation, in other categories; reservation
had to be spread evenly for the representation of women category
candidates to the extent of a minimum of 20 percent in each category;
in the event selections, as held by the respondents, were maintained,

21
this would amount to transfer of the horizontal slot of other categories
in excess of 20 percent for females in the other backward classes
category, which would be contrary to the terms and conditions of the
advertisement which did not allow enforcement of an overall
horizontal reservation; the advertisement clearly provided for
horizontal reservation category-wise; and the calculation in the

35. The Full Bench, thereafter, observed :
"Nonetheless, another facet of the matter is that the
women as a class include women of all social reserved
categories. No one can deny that a women of socially
reserved categories (S.C., S.T. & O.B.C.) belong to a less
advantaged group of the society than a women of Open
category. The short fall of vacancies, if filled, from each
social reserved category by adopting the method of
proportionate division of short fall or
compartmentalization, women of socially reserved
category who may be much below in the inter-se merit
list of women would get a chance for selection.
The question is, how to go about it? How to apply
reservation to fill the short fall under the
compartmentalization method?
Our solution is that instead of one merit lists, if
four lists are prepared to fill the short fall, by keeping
women of four social reserved categories (Open,
SC/ST, & OBC), separately, the process of
adjustment/placement would be much more simpler
and transparent. Where there is less representation of
women 'Overall', the selection agency has to turn to
the aforesaid lists to fill the short fall. Then the
proportionate representation of women in each social
category (S.C., S.T., OBC & Open) list prepared at
the first two stages of selection, as aforesaid, has to be
seen. If woman in the list of open category prepared
at the first stage are represented to the extent of 20%,
there will be no further question of adjustment or
displacement of their male counterpart to fill the
short fall. Similarly, in the list of OBC, SC, & ST,
prepared at the second stage of selection, where there
is less representation of women than 20% (in
proportion of the percentage of their reservation), the
placement/adjustment can be made up to that extent.
The short-fall has to be divided in that case
proportionately, as per the quota for vertical reserved

26
category i.e. 50% for Open category, 21% for S.C.,
27% for O.B.C. & 2% for S.T. (total 50%). But in any
case, "Overall" adjustment even by the said method
cannot be more than the seats reserved for women to
the extent of 20% of the total seats notified for
selection i.e. such adjustment/placement should not
result in breach of limit of 20% 'Overall' as the
question would be only to fill the short fall.
We are conscious that there may be a case
where it is not possible to get representation of women
in any one or two of the social categories i.e. SC, ST.,
OBC & Open category in a particular selection and in
compartmentalized method it is not possible to
transfer the remaining seats to another category, as
the special reservation in such a case shall be in a
water-tight compartment in each of the vertical
categories (Open, OBC, SC & S.T.) and the "Overall"
reservation of 20% of the total seats in favour of
women may yet to be honoured. But such a situation,
in our opinion, will not make much difference or
prejudice the women (special category) candidates as
women reservation is more on the principle of gender
equality to encourage their participation in socio-economic activities of the nation on the footing of
equality. The representation of women may be more than
adequate in another selection as they may take a sweep to
displace their male counterparts in the merit lists
prepared at the first and second stages itself, by
competing them on merit.
There is no constitutional or legal bar on the
State in categorizing women in social categories. Such
a categorization rather will be a balancing act which
will address the interest of both genders and prevent a
situation where the entire list of a particular social
category is replaced by displacing meritorious male
candidates to give place to women in that category. If
the "Overall" adjustment method to fill the short fall
by preparation of one inter-se merit list of women is
adopted, their representation or adjustment may be
possible only in one social category. Whereas, if
compartmentalization (proportionate division of seats
in social category) method is adopted women of all
social categories will get a fair chance for selection,
though may be lower in the common inter-se merit of
women. Thus, by applying reservation
proportionately in the social categories to fill up the
short fall, minimum damages is done to the merit and
maximum representation of women is secured. The
view taken by us is in the line of the need for women
empowerment by economic means and will also help
the marginalized women or women of economically

27
and socially less empowered group of SC, ST & OBC
categories to make their way to the select list.
For the analysis made above, keeping in view
the object and purpose of women reservation, we hold
that the method of compartmentalization (in
watertight compartment) or proportionate division of
seats reserved for women (horizontal reservation
category) to the extent of 20% in the social reserved
categories is the most preferred method and shall be
applied uniformly as a rule in all selections in the
State of U.P. under the scheme of the Government
order dated 26.02.1999."
36. The Full Bench concluded holding :
"Our answer to the question of implementation of
women reservation in the State of U.P. under the Scheme
of the Government order dated 26.02.1999 referred to
this Bench is thus, as under:-
(i) The observations in Anil Kumar Gupta
(supra) in paragraph no.'17' & '18' are followed and
reiterated to hold that the method of implementation
of horizontal reservation in favour of women in the
State of U.P. shall be a "compartmentalized
horizontal reservation" in the manner stated above,
so as to avoid any complication and intractable
problems in future.
(ii) The method of compartmentalization or
proportionate representation by dividing seats
reserved for women candidates amongst the vertical
(social) categories being in watertight compartment
and not inter-transferable, shall be the rule and
"Overall" method of implementation at the last stage
of filling the short fall shall be the exception, which
can be applied in a particular selection, after taking a
conscious decision by the State by notifying for
application of the said method, being "Overall", in
the advertisement itself.
(iii) At the first and second stages of
preparation of the merit lists of social categories,
there will be one method only which is "Overall"
calculation of seats secured by women candidates, (to
the extent of 20% of the total vacancies), irrespective
of their social categories. As occasion to apply women
reservation, by displacement of male candidates in a
selection will arise only after the said two stages are
over and in the event there is short fall. The reference
to the Larger Bench, accordingly, stands answered."

38. The Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court in Rajeev
Kumar8
and Ashish Kumar Pandey9
, and the Full Bench of the
Allahabad High Court in Ajay Kumar10, have followed the law
declared by the Supreme Court in Anil Kumar Gupta7
.
39. The law laid down in Anil Kumar Gupta7
 is that, unlike
vertical reservation where members of the scheduled castes, the
scheduled tribes, and the other backward classes, who have secured
appointment on their own merit, are required to be excluded while

29
filling up posts vertically reserved in favour of the scheduled castes,
the scheduled tribes and the other backward classes, the requirement
of a valid horizontal reservation would be satisfied if, in each
category, the percentage of posts, prescribed for the horizontally
reserved categories, are filled up. The question which also arose for
consideration therein was whether, in the process of filling up the
quota prescribed for the horizontally reserved category, transfer of
unfilled horizontally reserved posts, from one category to another,
was permissible.
40. The law laid down in Anil Kumar Gupta7
, can be better
explained by way of an illustration. For instance, if there are 100 posts
available to be filled up, of which 50 posts are under the general
category, 20 posts under the scheduled castes category, 20 posts under
the other backward classes category and 10 posts under the scheduled
tribes category, and if 20% overall reservation is required to be
horizontally provided for women i.e. for a total of 20 posts, then
reserving the entire 20 posts in the general category would result in
these 20 posts being filled up, among women, solely in their order of
merit, not only depriving men belonging to the general category but
also women, belonging to the schedule castes, the scheduled tribes
and the other backward classes, of appointment on the ground that
they were less meritorious than the women in the unreserved category;
and it was advisable that 20% posts, horizontally reserved in favour of
women, should also be distributed among each categories. In the
aforesaid illustration, it would then require 10 posts to be horizontally
reserved in favour of women under the general category, 4 posts each
for women in the scheduled castes and the other backward classes
categories, and two posts for women in the scheduled tribes category.
41. The difficulty which may still arise is in case posts reserved for
women, under the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the other
backward classes categories, remain unfilled because of non-availability of adequate women, eligible for appointment, under each
of these categories. The question which arose for consideration in

30
Anil Kumar Gupta7 was whether, in order to ensure that the
prescribed 20% quota horizontally reserved for women is filled up in
its entirety, it was permissible to transfer these horizontally reserved
unfilled posts, in the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the
other backward classes categories, to the general category to be filled
up by women not belonging to any of these vertically reserved
categories, thereby ensuring that the 20% quota, horizontally reserved
in favour of women, is completely filled up by women. Transfer of
such posts to the general category, to satisfy the 20% quota
horizontally reserved for women, would result in posts, reserved in
favour of the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the other
backward classes (albeit women in each of these categories) not being
available for the respective categories, and instead being taken away
by women not belonging to any of these categories i.e. women not
belonging to the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the other
backward classes.
42. As this process of transfer would result in posts reserved in
favour of the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the other
backward classes being transferred to the general category, which is
not only impermissible but would also reduce the number of posts
available to be filled up by persons belonging to these backward
classes, it was felt that these unfilled posts, reserved in favour of
women in the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes and the other
backward classes categories, should, ordinarily, not be transferred to
the general category, as, otherwise, the object of providing vertical
reservation in favour of these backward classes would be defeated.
43. It is in this context that certain observations were made in the
aforesaid judgments of the Allahabad High Court, which followed the
law laid down by the Supreme Court, both in Rajesh Kumar Daria3
and in Anil Kumar Gupta7
, that the method of compartmentalization
should be followed in horizontal reservation by dividing seats,
horizontally reserved among the vertical (social) categories, in
watertight compartments, and as not inter-transferable. That does not

31
mean that posts, horizontally reserved in the general category, is
unavailable for the backward classes i.e. the scheduled castes, the
scheduled tribes and the other backward classes belonging to the said
horizontal category. These horizontally reserved posts in the general
category are open to all candidates, belonging to the said horizontal
category, to be filled up on their inter-se merit.
44. In none of the judgments of the Supreme Court, referred to
hereinabove, has it been held that posts in the general category can be
filled up otherwise than by way of inter-se merit among all eligible
candidates irrespective of their caste or social status. Applying the
illustration, in Rajesh Kumar Daria3
, to the facts of the present case,
would have required the Public Service Commission to first arrange
all candidates strictly in the order of their inter-se merit. On doing so,
a merit list under the general category should have been prepared till
the last candidate who had secured 818 marks. The Commission was
then required to examine whether any of these candidates, who had
secured 818 marks or more, belonged to the ex-servicemen category
for whom one post was horizontally reserved under the general
category. On finding that there were none, the Commission was,
thereafter, required to substitute the candidate who secured 818 marks
with the most meritorious ex-serviceman lower in the merit list which,
in the present case, was the writ petitioner who had secured 807
marks. The Commission ought to have substituted the candidate who
secured 818 marks with the writ petitioner who was most meritorious
ex-serviceman. Instead, the Commission substituted the candidate
who secured 818 marks with the fourth respondent-review applicant
herein, who had only secured 776 marks (31 marks lesser than the
writ petitioner), on the ground that, while the writ petitioner belonged
to the scheduled castes, the fourth respondent-review applicant did not
belong to any of the backward classes (i.e. the vertically reserved
categories).
45. This exercise was carried out by the Commission on the
erroneous premise that posts, horizontally reserved in favour of ex-

32
servicemen under the general category, were unavailable to be filled
up from members of the backward classes (i.e. SC, ST and OBC),
even if they were found more meritorious than those who did not
belong to any of these backward sections entitled to vertical
reservation. Since posts in the general category, even those
horizontally reserved in favour of women, the physically handicapped,
the ex-servicemen etc, are available to all, who satisfy the criteria of
horizontal reservation, irrespective of their caste or social status, and
are to be filled up solely on the basis of their inter-se merit, we had
faulted the Commission in overlooking a more meritorious candidate
on the erroneous premise that, as he belonged to the scheduled castes,
he was ineligible to compete for posts horizontally reserved under the
general category, and instead a less meritorious candidate i.e. the
fourth respondent-review applicant should be selected and
recommended for appointment to the post horizontally reserved in
favour of ex-servicemen under the general category.
46. Reliance is placed, on behalf of the review applicant, on the
aforesaid judgments of the Allahabad High Court, to contend that,
since horizontal reservation is required to be provided to each
category in watertight compartments, posts horizontally reserved
under the general category are unavailable to the backward classes.
That is not what the Supreme Court has laid down in Anil Kumar
Gupta7
; Rajesh Kumar Daria3
 and Mamta Bisht5
. Stray
observations in the judgments of the Allahabad High Court cannot be
read out of context as a declaration of law inconsistent with the law
declared by the Supreme Court in the aforesaid judgments.
Observations of judges should neither be read as Euclid's theorems,
nor as provisions of a Statute. The observations must be read in the
context in which they appear. (M/s Amar Nath Om Prakash and
others15; Sreenivasa General Traders and ors. vs. State of Andhra
Pradesh and others16). To interpret words, phrases and provisions of
a Statute, it may become necessary for Judges to embark upon lengthy
discussions but the discussion is meant to explain, and not to define.

33
Judges interpret Statutes, they do not interpret judgments. They
interpret words of statutes, their words are not to be interpreted as
statutes [Haryana Financial Corpn. vs. Jagdamba Oil Mills17;
London Graving Dock Co. Ltd. vs. Horton18; Bharat Petroleum
Corporation Ltd vs. N.R. Vairamani19; Ashwani Kumar Singh vs.
U.P. Public Service Commission20; Union of India vs. Amritlal
Manchanda21; P Sridevi W/o P Murali Krishna vs. Cherishma
Housing Private Ltd22 and Deepak Bajaj vs. State of
Maharashtra23).There is always peril in treating the words of a
speech or a judgment as though they were words in a legislative
enactment, and it should be remembered that judicial utterances are
made in the setting of the facts of a particular case. (Herrington vs.
British Railways Board24; Ashwani Kumar Singh20; Collector of
Central Excise, Calcutta vs. Alnoori Tobacco Products25; Escorts
Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Delhi II26; N.R.
Vairamani19 and Union of India vs. Major Bahadur Singh27).
47. Observations of Courts should not be taken out of context.
Circumstantial flexibility, one additional or different fact may make a
world of difference between conclusions in two cases. (N.R.
Vairamani19; State of A.P. vs. M/s Seven Hills Constructions28).
A word here, or a word there, should not be made the basis for
inferring inconsistency or conflict of opinion. Law does not develop
in a casual manner. It develops by conscious, considered steps. (Sri
Konaseema Cooperative Central Bank Ltd vs. N. Seetharama
Raju29).
48. The submission that, since the writ petitioner had claimed the
benefit of reservation as a member of the scheduled castes, pursuant to
the advertisement whereby applications were invited for appointment
to the posts of Deputy Collectors, he cannot change his option to the
general category, is only to be noted to be rejected. A member of the
scheduled castes can opt not to claim the benefit of reservation under
the scheduled caste category and, if he so opts, he would then not be
entitled for appointment to posts reserved in favour of the scheduled

34
castes. The converse, however, is not true. No person need exercise
the option that he should be considered for appointment under the
general category for, even a scheduled caste candidate, who opts not
to claim the benefit of reservation as a member of the scheduled
castes, would, nonetheless, be entitled to be considered, along with all
other candidates, under the general category.
49. As noted hereinabove, posts in the general category are
available to all. No person needs to exercise his specific option that he
be considered for appointment under the general category. The
moment a person exercises option not to claim the benefit of
reservation, he would then automatically be entitled to be considered
under the general category. Even if a person claims the benefit of
reservation to posts, reserved in favour of the scheduled castes, he
would, nonetheless, be entitled to be considered for selection to posts
in the general category, as general category posts are open to all and
are not restricted only to those who are not members of the scheduled
castes, the schedules tribes, and the other backwards classes. The
contentions, based on the advertisement, therefore necessitate
rejection.
50. While hearing Writ Petition (S/B) No.392 of 2017, our attention
was drawn to the provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Public Services
(Reservation for Physically Handicapped, Dependants of Freedom
Fighters and Ex-Servicemen) Act, 1993. Sections 3(1) and 3(3) of the
said Act were, in fact, relied on behalf of the writ petitioner. We had
also taken note of the judgment of the Division Bench of the
Allahabad High Court in Brijendra Deo Mishra4
, wherein the
provisions of Section 3(1) and 3(3) of the 1993 Act were extensively
dealt with.
51. The contention now urged in the present review petition, that a
particular nuance of the provisions of the 1993 Act was not noticed,
would not justify this Court re-examining the matter all over again, for
it is well settled that, while Article 226 of the Constitution of India

35
does not preclude the High Court from exercising the power of review
which inheres in every Court of plenary jurisdiction to prevent
miscarriage of justice or to correct grave and palpable errors
committed by it, it would not be exercised on the ground that the
decision was erroneous on merits as that is the province of a court of
appeal. A power of review is not to be confused with the appellate
power which may enable an appellate court to correct all manner of
errors committed by the subordinate court. (Aribam Tuleshwar
Sharma vs. Aribam Pishak Sharma30; Meera Bhanja vs. Nirmala
Kumari Choudhury31; Mudiki Bhimesh Nanda vs. Tirupati Urban
Development Authority32). The dictionary meaning of the word
"review" is "the act of looking, offer something again with a view to
correction or improvement. The power of review can be exercised for
correction of a mistake and not to substitute a view. The mere
possibility of two views on the subject is not a ground for review.
(Lily Thomas vs. Union of India33; Mudiki Bhimesh Nanda32).
52. Review literally, and even judicially, means re-examination or
reconsideration. The basic philosophy inherent in it is the universal
acceptance of human fallibility. Yet, in the realm of law, Courts lean
strongly in favour of the finality of a decision - legally and properly
made. Exceptions have been carved out to judicially correct errors
which result in miscarriage of justice. (P. Neelakanteswaramma &
others vs. Uppari Muthamma & others34; Shivdeo vs. State of
Punjab35). An application for review would lie, inter alia, when the
order suffers from an error apparent on the face of the record, and
permitting the same to continue would lead to failure of justice. In the
absence of any such error, finality attached to the judgment/order
cannot be disturbed. The review court does not sit in appeal over its
own order. A rehearing of the matter is impermissible in law. It
constitutes an exception to the general rule that, once a judgment is
signed or pronounced, it should not be altered. Review is not an
appeal in disguise. (Inderchand Jain vs. Motilal36; Rajendra
Kumar vs. Rambai37 and Lily Thomas33).

36
53. An error, which is not self-evident and has to be detected by a
process of reasoning, can hardly be said to be an error apparent on the
face of the record justifying the court exercising its power of review.
In the exercise of the review jurisdiction, it is not permissible for an
erroneous decision to be "reheard and corrected". There is a clear
distinction between an erroneous decision and an error apparent on the
face of the record. While the first can be corrected by the higher
forum, the latter alone can be corrected by the exercise of the review
jurisdiction. (Parsion Devi vs. Sumitri Devi38; Mudiki Bhimesh
Nanda32). An error which is not self evident, and has to be detected
by a process of reasoning, can hardly be said to be an error apparent
on the face of the record justifying exercise of the power of review. A
review petition, it must be remembered, has a limited purpose.
(Haridas Das vs. Usha Rani Banik39).
54. A review lies only for correction of a patent error.
(Thungabhadra Industries vs. Govt. of A.P.40; Mudiki Bhimesh
Nanda32; Delhi Administration v. Gurdip Singh Uban41). The error
contemplated under the rule is not an error which is to be fished out
and searched. It must be an error of inadvertence. (Lily Thomas33). It
must be an error which must strike one merely on looking at the
record and not one which requires a long drawn process of reasoning
on points where there may conceivably be two opinions. (Meera
Bhanja31; Mudiki Bhimesh Nanda32; Satyanarayan Laxminarayan
Hegde vs. Mallikarjun Bhavanappa Tirumale42). There can be no
review unless the Court is satisfied that there exists a material error
manifest on the face of the earlier order resulting in miscarriage of
justice. (Avtar Singh v. Union of India43; P.
Neelakanteswaramma34).
55. An error, which necessitates review, should be something more
than a mere error and it must be one which must be manifest on the
face of the record. If the error is so apparent that, without further
investigation or enquiry, only one conclusion can be drawn in favour

37
of the petitioner, a review will lie. If the issue can be decided just by a
perusal of the records, and if it is manifest, it can be set right by
reviewing the order. If the judgment/order is vitiated by an apparent
error or it is a palpable wrong, and if the error is self evident, review
is permissible. (S. Bagirathi Ammal vs. Palani Roman Catholic
Mission44). A review proceeding cannot be equated with the original
hearing of the case and the finality of the judgment will be
reconsidered only where a glaring omission or patent mistake or like
grave error has crept in by judicial fallibility. (Northern India
Caterers vd. Lt. Governor Delhi45; Mudiki Bhimesh Nanda32). We
see no reason, therefore, to undertake the task of examining the
provisions of the 1993 Act again in the present review petition, for
that would amount to a rehearing of the Writ Petition itself, which is
impermissible.
56. Viewed from any angle, the order under review does not suffer
from any error, much less an error apparent on the face of the record,
necessitating exercise of our review jurisdiction. The review
application fails, and is, accordingly, dismissed. No costs.
